question:
Select the option that can be used as a one-word substitute for the underlined group of words.
My uncle is someone who loves good food and knows a lot about it.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Gourmet.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• A "Gourmet" is a person who loves good food and has expert knowledge and appreciation of fine food and drink. (भोजन का पारखी / स्वादिष्ट भोजन का शौकीन)
◦ Example: Being a true gourmet, she could tell exactly which spice was missing from the dish.

• The word is borrowed from French, where it originally meant a wine-taster's assistant, and later came to mean someone with a refined and discerning palate for food.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: Connoisseur (पारखी): A person with expert knowledge and taste in one of the fine arts, food/wine, or other cultural domains — a broader term not limited to food.

• Option 3: Chauffeur (चालक): A person employed to drive a private motor car.

• Option 4: Culinary (पाक-संबंधी): An adjective meaning "related to cooking or the kitchen" — it cannot substitute a phrase describing a person, since it does not denote a person.

NOTE

• Do not confuse "Gourmet" (a lover/connoisseur of good food) with "Gourmand" (a person who eats too much, a glutton) — these are frequently confused in SSC one-word substitution questions.

• Other food-related one-word substitutes: Epicure (one devoted to sensual, especially culinary, pleasure), Glutton (one who eats excessively).

question:
Sentences of a paragraph are given below in jumbled order. Arrange the sentences in the correct order to form a meaningful and coherent paragraph.
A. She participates in several functions and musical shows and receives accolades for her singing.
B. Vineeta has a very sweet voice which has inspired her to adopt singing as her profession.
C. She can also play musical instruments such as the sitar and the harmonium.
D. Now, she has opened a music school to train young singers.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. BACD.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Sentence B is the ideal opener as it introduces the subject, "Vineeta", and states the root cause of everything that follows — her sweet voice inspiring her to take up singing as a profession.

• Sentence A logically follows B, describing the immediate consequence of her taking up singing — she performs in functions and shows and earns accolades.

• Sentence C then adds further information about her musical ability (playing instruments), extending the description of her talent.

• Sentence D must come last, as the word "Now" signals a shift to the present/latest development — she has opened a music school, which is the culmination of her journey.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2, i.e., BACD.

Additional Information

• Option 1 (ADCB) is incorrect because it starts with A, whose pronoun "She" has no antecedent without B coming first.

• Option 3 (ACDB) is incorrect for the same reason — it starts with A instead of introducing Vineeta first through B.

• Option 4 (DCBA) is incorrect because it places the concluding sentence D ("Now, she has opened...") at the very start, which is illogical as nothing has been introduced yet.

NOTE

• In para-jumble questions, always identify the sentence that introduces the subject/proper noun for the first time (here, "Vineeta") — it is almost always the opening sentence, since every other sentence uses only the pronoun "She".

• Look out for linking/sequence words like "Now", "Also", "However", "Therefore" — they are strong clues to relative position within the paragraph.

question:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the given word.
Permeate
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Diffuse.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Permeate" means to spread throughout something; to pass into or through every part of a substance or place. (हर जगह फैल जाना / व्याप्त होना)
◦ Example: The smell of fresh coffee permeated the entire house.

• "Diffuse" (as a verb) means to spread out or disperse in every direction, to become dispersed throughout, which closely matches the meaning of "permeate". (फैलना)
◦ Example: The dye diffused slowly through the water until the whole glass turned blue.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: Exude (रिसना/झलकना): To discharge slowly, as if through pores (e.g., to ooze out a liquid or smell), or to display a quality strongly (e.g., "exude confidence") — it denotes emitting FROM a source, not spreading THROUGH something, so it is not an exact synonym.

• Option 2: Continue (जारी रखना): To carry on without stopping — unrelated to the idea of spreading through something.

• Option 3: Remain (शेष रहना): To stay in the same place or condition — this is nearly opposite in sense, since "permeate" implies active spreading, not staying static.

NOTE

• Other synonyms of "Permeate": Pervade, Saturate, Penetrate, Imbue, Suffuse.

• Do not confuse "Diffuse" (verb: to spread out) with "Diffident" (adjective: lacking self-confidence) — a common SSC trap.

question: Select the sentence that contains no spelling errors.
option_1: Anxiety is one of the most insidyous conditions affecting the mental health of an individual.
option_2: Anxiety is one of the most insidious conditions affecting the mental health of an individual.
option_3: Anxiety is one of the most insicdious conditions affecting the mental health of an individual.
option_4: Anxiety is one of the most insidiouos conditions affecting the mental health of an individual.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Anxiety is one of the most insidious conditions affecting the mental health of an individual.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The correct spelling is "Insidious" — meaning proceeding in a gradual, subtle way, but with harmful effects.

• Spelling key: IN + SID + I + OUS. Note the sequence "sid", followed by a single "i", and the ending "-ous" (not "-ouos" or "-yous"). The word comes from Latin insidiae, meaning "ambush" or "snare".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "insidyous" — incorrect; the "i" before "ous" has been wrongly replaced with "y".

• Option 3: "insicdious" — incorrect; an extra "c" has been wrongly inserted after "insi".

• Option 4: "insidiouos" — incorrect; an extra "o" has been wrongly inserted into the ending "-ous", making it "-ouos".

NOTE

• Other commonly confused "-ous" ending words in SSC spelling questions: Conscientious, Advantageous, Courageous, Outrageous, Simultaneous.

• Remember the general rule: adjectives ending in "-ous" are formed from Latin roots and rarely double letters unnecessarily — always check letter-by-letter against the root spelling when in doubt.

question:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the given word.
Answer
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Reply.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Answer" means a response given to a question, request, or problem, or, as a verb, to respond to someone. (उत्तर / जवाब देना)
◦ Example: She gave a quick answer/reply to his question.

• "Reply" carries the same core meaning — to say, write, or do something as a response — and can be used interchangeably with "answer" in most contexts. (जवाब)

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: Recall (याद करना): To bring a fact or memory back to mind — related to memory, not to responding.

• Option 3: Remember (याद रखना): To keep something in one's mind — again a memory-related word, not a synonym of "answer".

• Option 4: Query (प्रश्न/जिज्ञासा): A question or an expression of doubt — this is closer to the opposite of "answer" (a query is what prompts an answer), not a synonym.

NOTE

• Do not confuse words that ask (query, question) with words that respond (answer, reply, respond, retort) — SSC frequently sets "query" as a distractor for "answer"/"reply" questions.

• Other synonyms of "Answer": Respond, Retort, Rejoinder, Riposte (a quick, clever reply).

question:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.
She couldn't continue with a ________ diet to reduce her blood sugar.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. balanced.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "balanced" collocates fixedly with "diet" — "a balanced diet" is the standard term for a diet containing all the different types of food in the correct proportions needed to keep a person healthy.

• Since the sentence talks about a diet meant "to reduce her blood sugar", the diet being referred to is a properly proportioned, healthy diet — i.e., a balanced diet.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "practiced" does not collocate with "diet"; "practiced" is used for skills or habits (e.g., a practiced speaker), not for describing a type of diet.

• Option 2: "shortened" means made shorter in duration/length, which does not fit the sense of a diet plan meant to manage blood sugar.

• Option 3: "maintained" is grammatically odd here since it is a past participle used adjectivally and does not form a natural fixed phrase with "diet" the way "balanced diet" does.

NOTE

• Common fixed collocations tested by SSC: balanced diet, strict diet, crash diet, healthy diet, diet plan.

• Remember other food/health-related fixed phrases: "a nutritious meal", "a controlled diet", "to go on a diet".

question:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.
She has __________ her money and jewellery to help the poor.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. given away.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The phrasal verb "give away" means to donate or hand over something to someone else, typically without receiving payment. (मुफ्त में दान कर देना)
◦ Example: He gave away most of his fortune to charity before he died.

• Since the sentence describes the woman donating her money and jewellery to help the poor, "given away" is the correct phrasal verb to complete the sentence.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "give up" (छोड़ देना): Means to stop doing/having something or to surrender (e.g., "give up smoking") — it does not carry the sense of donating to someone else.

• Option 3: "give in" (हार मान लेना): Means to reluctantly agree to something after resisting, or to surrender/yield — unrelated to donating possessions.

• Option 4: "given way" (टूट जाना/रास्ता देना): Means to collapse or break under pressure, or to be replaced by something else — grammatically and semantically incorrect here.

NOTE

• Common "give" phrasal verbs tested by SSC: give away (donate/reveal a secret), give up (quit), give in (surrender), give out (distribute/run out), give off (emit, e.g., a smell or gas).

• "Give away" also has a second meaning: to accidentally reveal a secret (e.g., "his nervous laugh gave away the surprise").

question:
Select the correct spelling of the underlined word from the following options.
He deceaved the fraternity by the news of his unparalleled accomplishment to accommodate himself in the academic field.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. deceived.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The correct spelling is "Deceived" (past tense of "deceive") — meaning to mislead someone deliberately; to make someone believe something that is not true.

• Spelling key: remember the classic English rule "i before e except after c". Since the word begins with the letter sequence d-e-c, the "c" is immediately followed by "ei" — hence dec-EIVE-d, not "decieved".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "decieved" — incorrect; violates the "i before e except after c" rule by writing "ie" instead of "ei" after "c".

• Option 2: "desieved" — incorrect; the "c" has been wrongly replaced with an "s", and the letter order after it is also wrong.

• Option 3: "deseived" — incorrect; again the "c" has been wrongly replaced with an "s".

NOTE

• The "i before e except after c" rule applies to words like: receive, perceive, conceive, ceiling (ei after c), versus believe, achieve, relief, field (ie elsewhere).

• Related words to remember: Deceive (verb), Deceit (noun), Deceptive (adjective), Deception (noun).

question:
Select the correct passive form of the given sentence.
Uma told Susan to give up drinking.
option_1: Susan was told to give up smoking by Uma.
option_2: Susan is told to give up smoking by Uma.
option_3: Susan has been told to give up smoking by Uma.
option_4: Susan had been told to give up smoking by Uma.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Susan was told to give up smoking by Uma.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence "Uma told Susan to give up drinking" is in the Simple Past Tense, with the structure Subject + told + Object + to + Verb.

• Rule — Passive of "Subject + told/asked/ordered + Object + to + V1":
◦ Active: Subject + told + Object + to + V1
◦ Passive: Object + was/were + told + to + V1 + by + Subject

• Applying the rule: the object "Susan" becomes the subject; since it is singular and the tense is Simple Past, the auxiliary used is "was"; the infinitive phrase is retained as it is; and "Uma" becomes the agent introduced by "by".
◦ Passive: Susan was told to give up ... by Uma.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2 is incorrect because "is told" is the passive auxiliary of the Simple Present Tense, not the Simple Past Tense used in the original sentence.

• Option 3 is incorrect because "has been told" is the passive form of the Present Perfect Tense.

• Option 4 is incorrect because "had been told" is the passive form of the Past Perfect Tense, which requires two past actions with one occurring before the other — not applicable here.

NOTE

• With reporting verbs like told, asked, ordered, advised, requested followed by Object + to + V1, the passive is always formed as Object + be(was/were) + V3(told/asked/ordered) + to + V1 + by + Subject — the infinitive part after the object never changes.

• Always match the auxiliary verb's tense in the passive exactly to the tense of the main verb in the active sentence (told → was, not is/has been/had been).

question:
Select the correct indirect form of the given sentence.
Renu said to her brother, "You were watching the show without me."
option_1: Renu told her brother that he had been watching the show without her.
option_2: Renu told her brother that he has been watching the show without her.
option_3: Renu told her brother that he had watched the show without her.
option_4: Renu told her brother that he were watching the show without her.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Renu told her brother that he had been watching the show without her.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The reporting verb "said to" changes to "told" in indirect speech, and the reported clause requires the conjunction "that".

• Rule — Backshift of Past Continuous Tense: When the reporting verb is in the past tense, the Past Continuous Tense ("was/were + V-ing") in direct speech changes to the Past Perfect Continuous Tense ("had been + V-ing") in indirect speech.

• Applying the rule: "were watching" becomes "had been watching"; the pronoun "You" (referring to the brother) becomes "he"; and "me" becomes "her" (referring back to Renu).
◦ Indirect: Renu told her brother that he had been watching the show without her.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2 is incorrect because "has been watching" is a Present Perfect Continuous form, which is not the correct backshift of the Past Continuous Tense.

• Option 3 is incorrect because "had watched" is Past Perfect (simple), which loses the continuous/ongoing sense ("was watching") of the original sentence.

• Option 4 is incorrect because "he were watching" is grammatically wrong — "were" does not agree with the third-person singular subject "he" (it should be "was", and further backshifted to "had been").

NOTE

• Tense backshift chart for narration: Simple Present → Simple Past; Present Continuous → Past Continuous; Present Perfect → Past Perfect; Past Simple → Past Perfect; Past Continuous → Past Perfect Continuous.

• Pronoun changes must always be checked according to who is speaking, who is spoken to, and who is being referred to.

question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the given word.
Cacophony
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Symphony.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Cacophony" means a harsh, discordant mixture of sounds; unpleasant noise. (कर्कश शोर)
◦ Example: The cacophony of car horns during rush hour gave her a headache.

• "Symphony" here refers to a harmonious combination or arrangement of sounds; a pleasing agreement of sounds, which is directly opposite to the harshness implied by "cacophony". (सुरों का सामंजस्य/मधुर संगीत)
◦ Example: The wind chimes created a gentle symphony of tinkling notes.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: Colophony (राल/रोज़िन): A hard resin (rosin) obtained from pine trees, used for violin bows — completely unrelated in meaning to "cacophony" beyond a similar spelling.

• Option 2: Polyphony (बहुस्वरता): Music with two or more independent melodic lines/voices sounding together — describes a texture of music, not necessarily its pleasantness, so it is not a true opposite of "cacophony".

• Option 4: Antiphony (प्रत्युत्तर गान): Music or singing performed by two groups alternately responding to each other — again a description of musical form, not of harmoniousness, so it does not directly oppose "cacophony".

NOTE

• The most direct dictionary antonym of "cacophony" is "euphony" (a pleasant, harmonious sound); when "euphony" is not listed as an option, SSC often uses "symphony" as the closest available antonym.

• Related word: "Cacophonous" (adjective form, meaning harsh-sounding).

question:
The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
The audience has being / angry as the magician / is not performing / as expected.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. The audience has being.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The error lies in the phrase "has being". "Being" is the present participle/gerund form of "be" and cannot follow the auxiliary "has" in this construction.

• Rule: The Present Perfect Continuous requires "has/have been + V-ing", while a simple description of a present state/emotion (as intended here — "the audience is angry") requires the Simple Present auxiliary "is", not "has being".

• The corrected sentence should read: "The audience is angry as the magician is not performing as expected."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1 ("is not performing") is grammatically correct — a valid Present Continuous negative form describing an ongoing action.

• Option 2 ("as expected") is grammatically correct — a standard adverbial phrase of comparison.

• Option 4 ("angry as the magician") is grammatically correct in isolation — the adjective "angry" followed by the comparative conjunction "as" introducing the reason clause.

NOTE

• Do not confuse "has been" (correct auxiliary + past participle, used in Present Perfect) with the incorrect "has being" — "being" should only follow "is/am/are/was/were" (e.g., "he is being rude") or function as a gerund/noun (e.g., "seeing is believing"), never directly after "has/have".

• Common error-spotting trap: "has being" / "have being" are almost always wrong — the correct forms are either "has been" (perfect) or "is/are being" (continuous passive/temporary state).

question:
Rearrange the parts of the sentence in correct order.
Medieval people undertook
P. purify themselves of sin, to transform
Q. pilgrimages individually, travelling to
R. themselves through a trial of faith.
S. distant shrines as a penance to
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. QSPR.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The fixed opening "Medieval people undertook" must be followed by an object — "pilgrimages" — which appears in part Q, so Q comes first: "Medieval people undertook pilgrimages individually, travelling to..."

• Part Q ends with "travelling to", which needs a destination — this is completed by part S: "...distant shrines as a penance to..."

• Part S ends with "as a penance to", which needs a purpose (an infinitive verb) — this is completed by part P: "...purify themselves of sin, to transform..."

• Part P ends with "to transform", which needs an object and completion — this is completed by part R: "...themselves through a trial of faith."

• Full sentence: "Medieval people undertook pilgrimages individually, travelling to distant shrines as a penance to purify themselves of sin, to transform themselves through a trial of faith."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4, i.e., QSPR.

Additional Information

• Option 1 (PSRQ) is incorrect because it places P ("purify themselves of sin, to transform") right after the opening, which does not grammatically or logically follow "Medieval people undertook".

• Option 2 (QPRS) is incorrect because after "travelling to" (end of Q), it jumps to P, leaving "travelling to" without a destination.

• Option 3 (SPQR) is incorrect because it starts with S ("distant shrines as a penance to"), which cannot directly follow "Medieval people undertook".

NOTE

• In sentence-rearrangement questions, always locate the part that logically supplies the missing object/complement for the fixed opening or closing phrase given in the question — trace each dangling preposition or infinitive ("travelling to", "as a penance to", "to transform") to the part that completes it.

• Chain the parts like links: each part's ending phrase should grammatically demand what the next part supplies.

question:
Select the option that can be used as a one-word substitute for the given group of words.
One who can speak two languages
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Bilingual.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Bilingual" means a person who can speak two languages fluently. (द्विभाषी)
◦ Example: Growing up in Montreal, she became bilingual in English and French.

• The prefix "bi-" means "two" (as in bicycle, bimonthly), which directly matches "two languages" in the question.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: Multilingual (बहुभाषी): One who can speak many/several (more than two) languages.

• Option 3: Trilingual (त्रिभाषी): One who can speak three languages (prefix "tri-" = three).

• Option 4: Monolingual (एकभाषी): One who can speak only one language (prefix "mono-" = one).

NOTE

• Number-prefix word family frequently tested by SSC: mono- (one), bi-/di- (two), tri- (three), multi-/poly- (many).

• Related one-word substitutes: Polyglot (a person who knows and can use several languages), Linguist (a person who studies languages or knows several).

question:
The question below consists of a set of labeled sentences. Out of the four options given, select the most logical order of the sentences to form a coherent paragraph.
P. Honey ants are common in deserts and other arid climates around the world.
Q. They are part of the "worker" caste of honey ants.
R. Other castes include soldiers, who protect the colony from predators and the queen—usually is the mother of all other ants in the colony.
S. Only some honey ants become "living larders".
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. PSQR.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Part P is the ideal opener as it introduces the general topic — "Honey ants" and where they are commonly found — before any specific detail is discussed.

• Part S logically follows P, narrowing the focus from honey ants in general to the specific sub-group that becomes "living larders".

• Part Q follows S, using the pronoun "They" to refer back to the "living larders" just mentioned, and explains that they belong to the "worker" caste.

• Part R comes last, as it naturally extends the idea of "caste" introduced in Q by describing the "other castes" (soldiers and the queen) that exist besides the worker caste.

• Full order: P (general introduction) → S (narrows to living larders) → Q (explains their caste) → R (describes other castes).

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3, i.e., PSQR.

Additional Information

• Option 1 (RPQS) is incorrect because it starts with R, which discusses "other castes" — a detail that presupposes the reader already knows about the worker caste, which has not yet been introduced.

• Option 2 (RSPQ) is incorrect for the same reason — it opens with R before the topic of castes has been established by P, S, and Q.

• Option 4 (SQRP) is incorrect because it opens with S ("Only some honey ants..."), which assumes the reader already knows what honey ants are, without the general introduction given in P.

NOTE

• In paragraph formation, always look for the sentence that introduces the topic in general terms (here, P, naming "honey ants" and their habitat) — this is almost always the opening sentence.

• Track pronoun references ("They" in Q) and category words ("other castes" in R, which requires a caste to have already been named) to fix the logical chain.

question:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.
He's sitting on the fence
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. He can't take a decision.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "to sit on the fence" means to avoid committing oneself to either side of a debate or dispute; to remain neutral or undecided. (किसी निर्णय पर न पहुँचना / तटस्थ रहना)
◦ Example: The mayor has been sitting on the fence over the new construction project for months.

• The image behind the idiom is of a person literally sitting on top of a fence/boundary, unwilling to jump down on either side — symbolising indecisiveness.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1 (He can't stop trying) describes persistence, which is unrelated to the idiom's meaning of indecision.

• Option 2 (He can't do anything seriously) suggests frivolousness, which is not what the idiom conveys.

• Option 3 (He can't hide himself) relates to concealment, which has no connection with sitting on a fence.

NOTE

• Other idioms related to indecision often tested by SSC: "To blow hot and cold" (to keep changing one's opinion), "To be in two minds" (to be unable to decide), "To hum and haw" (to hesitate while speaking/deciding).

• Contrast with idioms of decisiveness: "To take the bull by the horns" (to face a difficult situation directly and with determination).

question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the given word.
Jeopardy
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Safety.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Jeopardy" means danger of loss, harm, or failure; a risky or perilous situation. (खतरा/जोखिम)
◦ Example: His careless driving put the lives of other passengers in jeopardy.

• "Safety" means the condition of being protected from or unlikely to cause danger, risk, or injury, which is the direct opposite of "jeopardy". (सुरक्षा)

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: Danger (खतरा): A near-synonym of "jeopardy" (a situation involving possible harm), not its opposite.

• Option 3: Precaution (सावधानी): A measure taken in advance to prevent harm — related to safety but describes an action, not a state, so it is a weaker antonym than "Safety" itself.

• Option 4: Risk (जोखिम): Also a near-synonym of "jeopardy" (exposure to the chance of harm), not its opposite.

NOTE

• Be careful not to confuse near-synonyms (danger, risk, peril, hazard) with the true antonym (safety, security) — SSC often places synonyms of the given word as distractors in antonym questions.

• Related legal phrase: "Double jeopardy" — being tried twice for the same offence.

question:
Parts of the following sentence have been given as options. Select the option that contains a grammatical error.
The meeting was held upon / for an hour / due to non-availability / of the committee members.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. The meeting was held upon.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The error lies in the phrase "held upon". The correct phrasal verb to indicate that an event was delayed/postponed is "held up", not "held upon".

• Rule: "Hold up" means to delay or obstruct the progress of something, matching the sense of the sentence (the meeting was delayed for an hour due to the non-availability of committee members). "Held upon" is not a standard phrasal verb in English.

• The corrected sentence should read: "The meeting was held up for an hour due to non-availability of the committee members."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1 ("of the committee members") is grammatically correct — a standard possessive/prepositional phrase.

• Option 2 ("due to non-availability") is grammatically correct — "due to" correctly introduces the reason/cause.

• Option 3 ("for an hour") is grammatically correct — a standard adverbial phrase of duration.

NOTE

• Common "hold" phrasal verbs tested by SSC: hold up (delay/rob), hold on (wait/grip), hold back (restrain/hesitate), hold off (postpone), hold out (endure/resist).

• Do not confuse "held up" (delayed) with "held on" (waited/continued) or the simple verb "held" (conducted, e.g., "the meeting was held in the hall").

question:
Select the correct active form of the given sentence.
Before she came all the work had been completed by me.
option_1: I will complete all my work before she came.
option_2: I had completed all my work before she came.
option_3: I completed all my work before she came.
option_4: I complete all my work before she came.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. I had completed all my work before she came.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The given sentence "all the work had been completed by me" is in the Past Perfect Passive ("had been + V3"), used because one past action (completing the work) occurred before another past action ("she came").

• Rule — Active of Past Perfect Passive:
◦ Passive: Object + had been + V3 + by + Subject
◦ Active: Subject + had + V3 + Object

• Applying the rule: the agent "by me" becomes the subject "I"; the auxiliary "had been" becomes "had"; and "completed" (already V3) is retained; "all the work" becomes the object.
◦ Active: I had completed all my work before she came.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1 is incorrect because "will complete" is Simple Future Tense, which contradicts the past time frame ("before she came") of the original sentence.

• Option 3 is incorrect because "completed" alone is Simple Past Tense, which fails to show that the completion happened before the other past action ("she came") — the Past Perfect "had completed" is needed to preserve that sequence.

• Option 4 is incorrect because "complete" is Simple Present Tense, which does not match the past time frame of the sentence at all.

NOTE

• Whenever two past actions are compared and one happens before the other, the earlier action must be in the Past Perfect Tense ("had + V3") — this rule holds in both active and passive voice.

• Time-marker words like "before", "after", "as soon as", "by the time" are strong clues for Past Perfect Tense usage.

question:
Select the option that can be used as a one-word substitute for the given group of words.
to give up completely or agree to forgo, especially in favour of another
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Surrender.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Surrender" means to give up completely, or to yield/hand over a right, claim, possession or position, especially to or in favour of another. (पूरी तरह छोड़ देना / समर्पण करना)
◦ Example: He surrendered his claim to the family property in favour of his younger brother.

• The phrase in the question combines two ideas — "give up completely" and "agree to forgo in favour of another" — both of which are core senses of "surrender" as used for rights, claims and possessions.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: Waive (माफ करना/त्याग देना): To voluntarily refrain from insisting on or using a right or claim (e.g., "waive a fee"); it emphasises choosing not to exercise a right, but does not itself carry the specific "especially in favour of another" nuance as strongly as "surrender".

• Option 2: Forfeit (दंडस्वरूप गंवाना): To lose or be deprived of something as a penalty for wrongdoing or failure to fulfil an obligation — this involves compulsion/penalty, not a voluntary agreement "in favour of another".

• Option 4: Cosign (सह-हस्ताक्षर करना): To sign a document jointly with another person, typically as a guarantor (e.g., co-signing a loan) — entirely unrelated in meaning to "giving up" something.

NOTE

• Distinguish carefully between near-synonyms of "give up": Waive (voluntarily not enforce a right), Forfeit (lose as a penalty), Surrender (give up completely/hand over, often in favour of someone else), Relinquish (formally give up a position/possession), Abdicate (formally give up a throne/responsibility).

• Related one-word substitutes: Concede (to admit or yield, especially after resistance), Renounce (to formally give up a title, claim or belief).

question:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

As writers we live life twice, like (1) _________ cow that eats its food once and then regurgitates it to chew and digest (2) _________ again. We have a second chance (3) _________ biting into our experience and examining it. This is our life and it's not going to last forever. There isn't time to talk about someday writing that short story or poem or novel. Slow down now, touch what is (4) _________ you, and out of care and compassion for (5) _________ moment and detail, put pen to paper and begin to write.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 1.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. a.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The blank requires an article before the singular countable noun "cow" in the phrase "like ___ cow that eats its food once...".

• Rule: The indefinite article "a" is used before a singular countable noun when it is being referred to in a general, non-specific sense (i.e., any cow in general, not a particular one already mentioned) — exactly the sense intended here, since the writer is drawing a general comparison.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1 ("any") is used in negative sentences, questions, or conditional clauses, or before plural/uncountable nouns to mean "no matter which" — it does not fit a simple affirmative comparison with a singular countable noun.

• Option 3 ("some") is generally used with plural or uncountable nouns, or to mean an unspecified quantity — it cannot precede the singular countable noun "cow" in this construction.

• Option 4 ("as") is a conjunction/preposition used for comparisons of manner or role (e.g., "as a teacher"), not an article, and cannot grammatically fill this determiner slot before "cow".

NOTE

• Use "a" before words beginning with a consonant sound, and "an" before words beginning with a vowel sound (e.g., "a cow", "an ant").

• Articles (a/an/the) are one of the most frequently tested categories in SSC cloze-passage questions — always check whether the noun is singular/plural, countable/uncountable, and specific/general.

question:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

As writers we live life twice, like (1) _________ cow that eats its food once and then regurgitates it to chew and digest (2) _________ again. We have a second chance (3) _________ biting into our experience and examining it. This is our life and it's not going to last forever. There isn't time to talk about someday writing that short story or poem or novel. Slow down now, touch what is (4) _________ you, and out of care and compassion for (5) _________ moment and detail, put pen to paper and begin to write.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 2.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. it.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The blank requires a pronoun that refers back to "its food", mentioned earlier in the same sentence — "...regurgitates it to chew and digest ___ again."

• Rule: A singular, previously-mentioned noun ("food") must be referred to using the singular object pronoun "it" to avoid needless repetition, maintaining cohesion within the sentence.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1 ("away") is an adverb meaning "to a distance"; it does not function as the object of the verb "digest" and makes no sense in this slot.

• Option 2 ("more") would suggest digesting an additional/greater quantity, which distorts the intended meaning of re-digesting the SAME food that was regurgitated.

• Option 4 ("a few") is used with plural countable nouns, but "food" is uncountable/singular here, so "a few" is grammatically incompatible.

NOTE

• In cloze passages, always trace pronouns back to their antecedent noun in the preceding clause to check number and gender agreement.

• Cohesive devices such as pronouns (it, they, this, that) are commonly tested to check whether a candidate can track reference across a sentence or passage.

question:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

As writers we live life twice, like (1) _________ cow that eats its food once and then regurgitates it to chew and digest (2) _________ again. We have a second chance (3) _________ biting into our experience and examining it. This is our life and it's not going to last forever. There isn't time to talk about someday writing that short story or poem or novel. Slow down now, touch what is (4) _________ you, and out of care and compassion for (5) _________ moment and detail, put pen to paper and begin to write.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 3.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. at.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The blank requires a preposition that correctly follows the fixed phrase **"a second chance ___ (doing something)"** — "We have a second chance ___ biting into our experience..."

• Rule: The idiomatic expression "a chance at (doing) something" uses the preposition "at" to indicate an opportunity to attempt or engage in an activity.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2 ("not") is a negator and makes no sense here, as it would negate having a second chance, contradicting the sentence's intended meaning.

• Option 3 ("beside") is a preposition of place meaning "next to", which is semantically inappropriate in this context of "chance".

• Option 4 ("about") does not idiomatically collocate with "a second chance" in the sense of an opportunity to do something; "about" would instead suggest the chance concerns/relates to the topic, which doesn't fit as naturally as "at".

NOTE

• Common fixed preposition collocations with "chance": a chance at (doing something), a chance of (something happening), by chance (accidentally), take a chance (on something).

• Preposition usage after abstract nouns like "chance", "opportunity", "reason" is a frequently tested cloze-passage category in SSC exams.

question:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

As writers we live life twice, like (1) _________ cow that eats its food once and then regurgitates it to chew and digest (2) _________ again. We have a second chance (3) _________ biting into our experience and examining it. This is our life and it's not going to last forever. There isn't time to talk about someday writing that short story or poem or novel. Slow down now, touch what is (4) _________ you, and out of care and compassion for (5) _________ moment and detail, put pen to paper and begin to write.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 4.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. around.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The blank requires a word that completes the phrase **"touch what is ___ you"**, meaning the writer's immediate surroundings and experiences.

• Rule: "Around" is a preposition meaning "on every side of; surrounding", and the phrase "what is around you" idiomatically means "your surroundings" or "everything present near/about you" — exactly the sense required in context (touch/engage with what is present in your life, right now).

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2 ("neither") is a negative correlative conjunction used with "nor" (e.g., "neither this nor that"); it cannot grammatically fill a simple prepositional slot after "is".

• Option 3 ("besides") means "in addition to", which does not fit the sense of touching what surrounds you in the present moment.

• Option 4 ("above") means "at a higher position than", which is spatially inaccurate and does not match the intended meaning of one's immediate surroundings.

NOTE

• The phrase "what is around you" is a common idiomatic way of referring to one's immediate environment/surroundings — frequently tested in reading-comprehension and cloze contexts.

• Do not confuse prepositions of surrounding (around, about) with prepositions of addition (besides) or position (above, below).

question:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

As writers we live life twice, like (1) _________ cow that eats its food once and then regurgitates it to chew and digest (2) _________ again. We have a second chance (3) _________ biting into our experience and examining it. This is our life and it's not going to last forever. There isn't time to talk about someday writing that short story or poem or novel. Slow down now, touch what is (4) _________ you, and out of care and compassion for (5) _________ moment and detail, put pen to paper and begin to write.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 5.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. each.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The blank requires a determiner before the singular phrase "moment and detail" — "...out of care and compassion for ___ moment and detail..."

• Rule: "Each" is used before a singular noun to mean "every individual one, considered separately", which matches the sense here — showing care and compassion for every single moment and every single detail, one at a time.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2 ("both") is used to refer to two specific things already identified (e.g., "both moments"), not to an open, general set of moments and details as intended here.

• Option 3 ("few") is used with plural countable nouns to mean "not many" (e.g., "few moments"), and does not fit before the singular "moment and detail".

• Option 4 ("little") is used with uncountable nouns to mean "not much" (e.g., "little time"), which contradicts the sentence's positive sense of valuing every moment and detail.

NOTE

• "Each" and "every" are both followed by singular nouns and singular verbs, but "each" can refer to as few as two items considered individually, while "every" implies three or more items considered collectively.

• Determiner usage before singular vs. plural vs. uncountable nouns (each/every vs. few/many vs. little/much) is a recurring SSC cloze-test category.
